claim: Impaired IFN-I response dynamics leads to the pathogenesis of a plethora of diseases that go beyond antiviral immunity only.
source: Crucial is the tight and well-orchestrated control of cellular decision-making leading to the production of IFN-I, as impaired response dynamics leads to the pathogenesis of a plethora of diseases that go beyond antiviral immunity only (Musella et al., 2017; Park and Iwasaki, 2020; Psarras et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Musella et al., 2017; Park and Iwasaki, 2020; Psarras et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020

claim: The initiation of IFN-I production is limited to only fractions of 1–3% of the total population, both found in vitro, in vivo, and across cell types.
source: Innovative single-cell approaches revealed that the initiation of IFN-I production is limited to only fractions of 1–3% of the total population, both found in vitro, in vivo, and across cell types, which were thought to be stochastically regulated.
evidence: Supported by references to single-cell approaches and observations across different experimental conditions

claim: Early IFN-I responders were thought to be stochastically regulated.
source: Innovative single-cell approaches revealed that the initiation of IFN-I production is limited to only fractions of 1–3% of the total population, both found in vitro, in vivo, and across cell types, which were thought to be stochastically regulated.
evidence: Represents the prevailing view in the field prior to this study

claim: Epigenetic drugs influenced the percentage of responding cells.
source: Epigenetic drugs influenced the percentage of responding cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Transient heritability drives responder fates during early IFN-I responses.
source: Next, with the classical Luria–Delbrück fluctuation test, we provided evidence for transient heritability driving responder fates, which was verified with mathematical modeling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fluctuation test and mathematical modeling

claim: Cell density plays an important role in dictating responsiveness during early IFN-I responses, similar to the phenomenon of quorum sensing.
source: Finally, while studying varying cell densities, we substantiated an important role for cell density in dictating responsiveness, similar to the phenomenon of quorum sensing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on varying cell densities

claim: IFN-I responses are elicited by fractions of so-called first responding cells, validated in vitro, in vivo, and across cell types.
source: In short, IFN-I responses are elicited by fractions of so-called first responding cells, also referred to as 'precocious cells' or 'early responding cells', which start the initial IFN-I production upon viral detection, both validated in vitro, in vivo, and across cell types (Bauer et al., 2016; Hjorton et al., 2020; Patil et al., 2015; Shalek et al., 2014; Van Eyndhoven et al., 2021a; Wimmers et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: First responders' IFN-I production is enhanced via autocrine signaling, inducing a feedforward loop resulting in the upregulation of IRF7 and other signaling components.
source: Their IFN-I production is further enhanced via autocrine signaling, inducing a feedforward loop resulting in the upregulation of interferon regulatory factor (IRF) 7 and other signaling components (Honda et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Honda et al., 2006

claim: First responders trigger additional IFN-I production in second responders, which are activated upon IFN-mediated paracrine signaling in combination with viral detection.
source: Simultaneously, first responders trigger additional IFN-I production in so-called second responders, which are activated upon IFN-mediated paracrine signaling in combination with viral detection (Van Eyndhoven et al., 2021b; Wimmers et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Van Eyndhoven et al., 2021b and Wimmers et al., 2018

claim: The early phase of IFN-I responses is currently thought to orchestrate population-wide IFN-I signaling and is crucial for establishing systemic antiviral protection.
source: Especially, the regulation of the early phase is of increasing interest, because this phase is currently thought to orchestrate population-wide IFN-I signaling, therefore of crucial importance in establishing systemic antiviral protection (Patil et al., 2015; Van Eyndhoven et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Patil et al., 2015 and Van Eyndhoven et al., 2021b

claim: A stochastic process is characterized by the exact same stimulus leading to varying response outcomes, often as a result of varying host-intrinsic factors.
source: In fact, a stochastic process in characterized by the exact same stimulus leading to varying response outcomes, often as a result of varying host-intrinsic factors (Symmons and Raj, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Symmons and Raj, 2016

claim: A deterministic process is characterized by an outcome that is fixed, or at least to a large degree, while the input can be variable.
source: In contrast, a deterministic process is characterized by an outcome (e.g., IFN-I production) that is fixed, or at least to a large degree, while the input can be variable.
evidence: Represents a conceptual definition used in the manuscript

claim: The later IFN-I phase seems mainly driven by stochastic processes, as the outcome is highly heterogeneous, mainly dictated by limiting host-intrinsic factors.
source: Accordingly, the later IFN-I phase seems mainly driven by stochastic processes, as the outcome is highly heterogeneous, mainly dictated by limiting host-intrinsic factors (e.g., intrinsic and extrinsic gene expression noise), and matching the course of an infection (Abadie et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abadie et al., 2019 and inference from the characteristics described

claim: Overexpression of signaling intermediates such as RIG-I, IRF3, and IRF7 leads to increased overall production of IFN-Is.
source: The limiting host-intrinsic factors can be manipulated by overexpression of signaling intermediates, such as retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I), IRF3, and IRF7, leading to an increased overall production of IFN-Is (Harrison and Moseley, 2020; Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harrison and Moseley, 2020 and Zhao et al., 2012

claim: Recent evidence suggests that the early phase, and more specifically the first responders, could be dictated by determinism instead of stochasticity.
source: In contrast, recent evidence suggests that the early phase, and more specifically the first responders, could be dictated by determinism instead (Bagnall et al., 2020; Shaffer et al., 2020; Talemi and Höfer, 2018; Van Eyndhoven et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bagnall et al., 2020; Shaffer et al., 2020; Talemi and Höfer, 2018; Van Eyndhoven et al., 2021a

claim: A transiently heritable gene expression program related to IFN-I signaling, including the expression of RIG-I (DDX58), IFIT1, PMAIP1, and OASL, was discovered to be initiated only in fractions of unstimulated cells.
source: Accordingly, a transiently heritable gene expression program related to IFN-I signaling, including the expression of RIG-I (DDX58), IFIT1, PMAIP1, and OASL, was discovered to be initiated only in fractions of unstimulated cells (Shaffer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shaffer et al., 2020

claim: Transient heritability refers to heritable epigenetic profiles that only transfer over a couple of generations.
source: Transient heritability refers to heritable epigenetic profiles (e.g., profiles encoding cellular fates for the production IFN-Is) that only transfer over a couple of generations, as observed across cell types and systems including cancer drug resistance (Shaffer et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2010), cancer fitness (Fennell et al., 2022; Oren et al., 2021), NK cell memory (Rückert et al., 2022), HIV reactivation in T cells (Lu et al., 2021), epithelial immunity (Clark et al., 2021), and trained immunity (Katzmarski et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work across different systems

claim: Numerous studies characterized epigenetic control of IFN-I-related genes (e.g., IFNB), which may be of crucial importance during the early phase of IFN-I response dynamics.
source: Moreover, numerous studies characterized epigenetic control of IFN-I-related genes (e.g., IFNB), which may be of crucial importance during the early phase of IFN-I response dynamics (Daman and Josefowicz, 2021; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Daman and Josefowicz, 2021 and Gao et al., 2021

claim: The effects of population density, often referred to as quorum sensing, are getting more established for immune signaling systems.
source: Besides a growing body of evidence on the role of transient heritable fates dictating cellular behaviors, the effects of population density, often referred to as quorum sensing, are getting more established for immune (signaling) systems (Antonioli et al., 2019; Polonsky et al., 2018; Van Eyndhoven and Tel, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Antonioli et al., 2019; Polonsky et al., 2018; Van Eyndhoven and Tel, 2022

claim: Quorum sensing can be considered a phenomenon in which autocrine cells determine their population density based on cells engaging in neighbor communication, but without self-communication.
source: In essence, quorum sensing can be considered a phenomenon in which autocrine cells determine their population density based on cells engaging in neighbor communication, but without self-communication (Doğaner et al., 2016; Van Eyndhoven and Tel, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doğaner et al., 2016 and Van Eyndhoven and Tel, 2022

claim: In the presence of competitive decision makers (i.e., cytokine consumers and producers), it is critical for individual cells to assess cellular density and act accordingly.
source: Especially in the presence of other competitive decision makers (i.e., cytokine consumers and producers), it is critical for individual cells to assess cellular density, and act accordingly (Oyler-Yaniv et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oyler-Yaniv et al., 2017

claim: The NIH3T3:IRF7-CFP reporter cell line expresses low, physiological background levels of IRF7-CFP fusion proteins.
source: Accordingly, we used a NIH3T3:IRF7-CFP reporter cell line, expressing low, physiological background levels of IRF7-CFP fusion proteins, to monitor signaling dynamics during early phase IFN-I response dynamics (Figure 1B).
evidence: Describes the characteristics of the cell line used in the study

claim: For the NIH3T3:IRF7-CFP cell model, IRF7 translocation correlates with IRF3 translocation.
source: For this cell model, IRF7 translocation correlates with IRF3 translocation, making IRF7 translocation as only readout sufficient to study first responders (Rand et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rand et al., 2012

claim: The response peaked at 7-hr post transfection, with an average of 2.1% of responding cells.
source: Accordingly, upon transfection optimization, in our experiments the response peaked at 7-hr post transfection, with an average of 2.1% of responding cells (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and 2F

claim: The percentage of early responders (2.1%) is in line with what has been found across literature, species (i.e., human and mice) and cell types (i.e., fibroblasts, monocyte-derived DCs, plasmacytoid DCs), which ranges from 0.8 to 10%.
source: This percentage is in line with what has been found across literature, species (i.e., human and mice) and cell types (i.e., fibroblasts, monocyte-derived DCs, plasmacytoid DCs), which ranges from 0.8 to 10% of early responders, emphasizing the elegant yet robust feature of only a fraction of first responding cells driving the population-wide IFN-I system (Bauer et al., 2016; Drayman et al., 2019; Patil et al., 2015; Shalek et al., 2014; Van Eyndhoven et al., 2021a; Wimmers et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work across different species and cell types

claim: At 7-hr post infection, clusters of STAT1/STAT2 translocated cells were captured in the NIH3T3:STAT1-CFP/STAT2-YFP fibroblast reporter cell line.
source: Accordingly, at 7-hr post infection, we were able to capture clusters of STAT1/STAT2 translocated cells (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I

claim: The clusters of STAT1/STAT2 translocated cells represent a phenomenon of competition between cytokine diffusion and consumption generating spatial niches of high cytokine concentrations with sharp boundaries.
source: The clusters represent a phenomenon of competition between cytokine diffusion (i.e., IFN-Is produced by first responder) and consumption (i.e., by surrounding cells) generating spatial niches of high cytokine concentrations with sharp boundaries (Oyler-Yaniv et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oyler-Yaniv et al., 2017 and inference from the observed pattern

claim: There is only a very low, though significant, correlation between responsiveness (IRF7 translocation ratio) and the actual amount of stimulus received by the cells (R2 = 0.0171, p < 0.0001).
source: To test the effect of a variety of extrinsic factors on the first responders, we first tested for a correlation between the responsiveness (i.e., IRF7 translocation ratio) and the actual amount of stimulus received by the cells, which was only very low, though significant (R2 = 0.0171, p < 0.0001) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: First responders are only minorly, if at all, influenced by stimulus dosage.
source: While the events displaying the highest IRF7 translocation ratios (above 2) only displayed very low levels of Poly(I:C) mean intensities, we conclude that first responders are only minorly, if at all, influenced by stimulus dosage.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing weak correlation between stimulus amount and response

claim: There is only a very weak correlation between IRF7 translocation ratio and IRF7 mean intensity (R2 = 0.0620, p < 0.0001).
source: However, we could only find a very weak correlation between IRF7 translocation ratio and IRF7 mean intensity (R2 = 0.0620, p < 0.0001), arguing that first responders are only minorly driven by differences in background levels of IRF7 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: There is significant heterogeneity in background IRF7 expression levels.
source: Although, it was interesting to observe the degree of heterogeneity in background IRF7 expression levels, as well as the significant increase in signal after stimulation (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: There is a significant increase in IRF7 signal after stimulation.
source: Although, it was interesting to observe the degree of heterogeneity in background IRF7 expression levels, as well as the significant increase in signal after stimulation (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Serum starvation for 24 hr induces a cell cycle arrest, halting cells in the G0/G1 phase, thereby synchronizing the whole population.
source: To explore the effect of cell cycle state on first responding cells, we aimed to synchronize the cells using serum starvation for 24 hr (Figure 3D). This approach induces a cell cycle arrest, halting cells in the G0/G1 phase, thereby synchronizing the whole population (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2012

claim: Only half of the cell numbers could be detected after 24-hr serum starvation, compared to the corresponding control samples.
source: We validated the cell cycle arrest by comparing the cell counts of starved conditions with unstarved conditions, which in theory should differ a factor of 2, knowing the cells divide approximately every 24 hr. Indeed, only half of the cell numbers could be detected after 24-hr serum starvation, compared to the corresponding control samples (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The percentage of first responding cells obtained from the starved conditions did not significantly differ from the percentages obtained from the unstarved conditions.
source: Interestingly, the percentage of first responding cells obtained from the starved conditions did not significantly differ from the percentages obtained from the unstarved conditions, suggesting that there is no significant effect of cell cycle state on first responders (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: There is no significant effect of cell cycle state on first responders.
source: Interestingly, the percentage of first responding cells obtained from the starved conditions did not significantly differ from the percentages obtained from the unstarved conditions, suggesting that there is no significant effect of cell cycle state on first responders (Figure 3F).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing no significant difference between starved and unstarved conditions

claim: The background levels of IRF7 were statistically significantly lower for the starved conditions, compared to the unstarved conditions.
source: Additionally, the background levels of IRF7 were (statistically) significantly lower for the starved conditions, compared to the unstarved conditions, again validating our successful approach of starving the cells, which limits the overall protein synthesis (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: For the majority of sister cells, the translocation ratios were remarkably similar.
source: Interestingly, comparing the two sister cells, the background levels of IRF7 only occasionally differed drastically (Figure 4A), whereas for the majority of sister cells the translocation ratios were remarkably similar (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: A similar phenomenon on a greater intra- than inter-lineage transcriptional similarity has been observed for CD8+ lymphocyte differentiation, which is also considered to be a deterministic process.
source: Accordingly, a similar phenomenon on a greater intra- than inter-lineage transcriptional similarity has been observed for CD8+ lymphocyte differentiation, which is also considered to be a deterministic process (Kimmerling et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kimmerling et al., 2016

claim: An average of 22.85% of responding cells are responding sister cells.
source: In theory, with an average of 22.85% of responding sister cells, it implies that two responding sister cells originated from one mother cell in 22.85% of the cases (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D

claim: Cells treated with DNMTis showed higher percentages of first responding cells.
source: Indeed, cells treated with DNMTis showed higher percentages of first responding cells, arguing that the cellular decision to become a responder is, at least partly, epigenetically regulated (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The cellular decision to become a responder is, at least partly, epigenetically regulated.
source: Indeed, cells treated with DNMTis showed higher percentages of first responding cells, arguing that the cellular decision to become a responder is, at least partly, epigenetically regulated (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing increased response rates with epigenetic drug treatment

claim: Treatment with varying dosages and durations of Trichostatin A, an histone deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi), increased the number of responding cells.
source: Also the treatment with varying dosages and durations of Trichostatin A, an histone deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi), increased the number of responding cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data mentioned in the text

claim: Unstimulated cells treated with epigenetic drugs showed increased percentages of responding cells, with even higher percentages upon DNMTi treatment compared to the stimulated DNMTi-treated cells.
source: However, unstimulated cells treated with epigenetic drugs also showed increased percentages of responding cells, with even higher percentages upon DNMTi treatment compared to the stimulated DNMTi-treated cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: DNMTis trigger cytosolic sensing of double stranded RNA originating from retroviruses that are no longer silenced while using these types of drugs.
source: This might be explained by the effect of DNMTis triggering cytosolic sensing of double stranded RNA originating from retroviruses, that are no longer silenced while using these types of drugs (Chiappinelli et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chiappinelli et al., 2015

claim: Unstimulated, DNMTi-treated cells showed increased levels of IRF7 mean intensities compared to unstimulated untreated cells.
source: We later confirmed this by showing increased levels of IRF7 mean intensities in unstimulated, DNMTi-treated cells, compared to unstimulated untreated cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claim: From generation 6 onwards, the probability of at least one responder being present becomes considerably high.
source: Assuming first responders are purely stochastically regulated, probability calculations can predict from which generation number the probability of at least one first responder present is close to one, knowing that on average only 2.134% first responders are present in a population (see Materials and methods). From generation 6 onwards, the probability of at least one responder being present becomes considerably high.
evidence: Calculated from probability theory based on observed response rate

claim: Each clone of generation 6, consisting of ~64 cells, would have 1.37 responding cells on average.
source: Subsequently, each clone, consisting of ~64 cells, would have 1.37 responding cells on average.
evidence: Calculated from probability theory based on observed response rate and expected cell numbers

claim: The majority (14/18) of generation 1 clones (consisting of two cells) showed 100% responsiveness.
source: Interestingly, the early generation clones showed remarkably high fractions of responders. In fact, the majority (14/18) of generation 1 clones (consisting of two cells) showed 100% responsiveness (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: With increasing generation numbers, corresponding with increasing cell numbers, the percentage of responders dropped drastically.
source: With increasing generation numbers, corresponding with increasing cell numbers, the percentage of responders dropped drastically (Figure 5C, D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–D; Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, D and supplementary figures

claim: From generation 13 onwards, the percentage of responders did no longer differ significantly compared to the regular clones (generation ꝏ).
source: From generation 13 onwards, the percentage of responders did no longer differ significantly compared to the regular clones (generation ꝏ).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: Up till clones of generation 6, the fluctuation across clones was rather large, with some clones showing no single translocation event.
source: In our experiments, up till clones of generation 6, the fluctuation across clones was rather large, with some clones showing no single translocation event.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The rather long timescales of switching from responders to nonresponders, and the other way around, imply epigenetic mechanisms at play.
source: The rather long timescales of switching from responders to nonresponders, and the other way around, imply epigenetic mechanisms at play, and indeed, prior work has indicated an important role for epigenetics dictating IFN-I response dynamics (reviewed in Barrat et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the observed timescales and supported by citation to Barrat et al., 2019

claim: The results from the fluctuation assay indicate a yet unknown, deterministic phenomenon which dictates responsiveness, which seems to overrule stochasticity.
source: Altogether, the results from the fluctuation assay indicate a yet unknown, deterministic phenomenon which dictates responsiveness, which seems to overrule stochasticity.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results of the fluctuation assay

claim: The transient heritability model could be fit to the data when starting from 100% responders at generation 0.
source: We could fit the transient heritability model to the data when starting from 100% responders at generation 0 (i.e., a single cell isolated from the regular culture).
evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results

claim: Cells switch OFF after five generation on average, with a constant kon rate throughout.
source: Cells switch OFF after five generation on average, with a constant kon rate throughout.
evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results

claim: In generation 0, nearly only IFN-I responders were observed.
source: Interestingly, in generation 0 we observed (nearly) only IFN-I responders, which we believe might be caused by single cells being deprived from any paracrine cues, which could include inhibitory factors that normally limited responsiveness.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Single cells may be deprived from paracrine cues, which could include inhibitory factors that normally limit responsiveness.
source: Interestingly, in generation 0 we observed (nearly) only IFN-I responders, which we believe might be caused by single cells being deprived from any paracrine cues, which could include inhibitory factors that normally limited responsiveness.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed high responsiveness in generation 0

claim: Single IFN-I-producing cells (i.e., plasmacytoid DCs and monocyte-derived DCs) encapsulated in picoliter droplets or captured in small microfluidic chambers did not display high responsiveness behavior.
source: However, single IFN-I-producing cells (i.e., plasmacytoid DCs and monocyte-derived DCs) encapsulated in picoliter droplets or captured in small microfluidic chambers did not display this behavior (Shalek et al., 2014; Wimmers et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shalek et al., 2014 and Wimmers et al., 2018

claim: Single cells seeded for cloning lack biochemical, and perhaps biomechanical cues provided by dense cell populations, which result in behavioral changes in these cells, making them more responsive.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that these single cells lack biochemical, and perhaps biomechanical cues provided by dense cell populations, which result in behavioral changes in these cells, in our case, making them more responsive.
evidence: Hypothesized explanation for the observed high responsiveness in single cells

claim: In quorum sensing, cells secrete soluble signaling molecules (called autoinducers), which enables cells to get a sense of their cell density.
source: Similarly, in quorum sensing, cells secrete soluble signaling molecules (called autoinducers), which enables cells to get a sense of their cell density (Postat and Bousso, 2019; Waters and Bassler, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Postat and Bousso, 2019 and Waters and Bassler, 2005

claim: In microfluidic droplets and chambers, autoinducer molecules accumulate, given the relatively small volumes.
source: In microfluidic droplets and chambers, these molecules accumulate, given the relatively small volumes.
evidence: Inferred from the physical constraints of microfluidic systems

claim: Transient heritability drives cellular decision-making during early IFN-I responses, as validated by mathematical modeling.
source: Together, we validated transiently heritable cellular decision-making driving responders using mathematical modeling.
evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results

claim: A small population of cells needs to contribute to greater extend, involving relatively more responders, than a large population of cells, to ensure the overall IFN-I production is similar.
source: Accordingly, a small population of cells needs to contribute to greater extend, involving relatively more responders, than a large population of cells, to ensure the overall IFN-I production is similar.
evidence: Logical inference about the relationship between cell density and response rates

claim: Cellular decision-making is defined by epigenetic profiling, which allows switching over time between a responding and nonresponding state, even before stimulation, and is subject to the phenomenon of quorum sensing.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that cellular decision-making is defined by epigenetic profiling, which allows switching over time between a responding and nonresponding state, even before stimulation, and is subject to the phenomenon of quorum sensing.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the integration of epigenetic and quorum sensing observations

claim: Single clones of generation 6 displayed high fluctuation, which closely matched with the data obtained earlier (average of 10.67 compared to 10.81; CV of 0.87 compared to 1.04, respectively).
source: The results confirmed that single clones of generation 6 displayed high fluctuation, which closely matched with the data obtained earlier (average of 10.67 compared to 10.81; CV of 0.87 compared to 1.04, respectively) (Figure 7F).

claim: The averages of merged clones of generation 6 displayed percentages of responding cells which closely matched with the numbers obtained from regular cultures (1.96% compared to 2.13, respectively).

claim: Cellular decision-making during early IFN-I responses is likely affected by the effects of quorum sensing.
source: To conclude, we confirm that cellular decision-making during early IFN-I responses is likely affected by the effects of quorum sensing.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results on cell density effects

claim: Cells seem to be aware of their density, and adjust their epigenetic profiling to allow their secretory behaviors accordingly.
source: In other words, cell seems to be aware of their density, and adjust their epigenetic profiling to allow their secretory behaviors accordingly (Figure 7G).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results on cell density effects

claim: The cellular decision to become a first responder can be considered as a fate, likely driven by a distinct epigenetic profile, rather than a coincidence driven by stochastic factors.
source: Here, we assessed the role of host-intrinsic factors dictating early IFN-I response dynamics. We observed that the cellular decision to become a first responder can be considered as a fate, likely driven by a distinct epigenetic profile, rather than a coincidence driven by stochastic factors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study

claim: The fate to become a first responder seems transiently heritable, of which the timescale indicates epigenetic mechanisms at play.
source: Furthermore, this fate seems transiently heritable, of which the timescale indicates epigenetic mechanisms at play, which is in line with the results obtained using epigenetic drugs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results and mathematical modeling

claim: The overall consensus on how first responders were thought to be regulated was by stochastic regulation, which is now challenged.
source: Previously, the overall consensus on how first responders were thought to be regulated was by stochastic regulation, or in other words randomly, which is now challenged (Wimmers et al., 2018).

claim: First responders are predetermined, meaning that their epigenetic profile is driving their responder fate.
source: In contrast, we currently hypothesize that first responders are predetermined, meaning that their epigenetic profile is driving their responder fate.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the experimental results of the study

source: The phenomenon of a small fraction of first responders, responsible for the rapid and robust production of IFN-Is, has been observed across species and cell types.

claim: Various stimuli (live and synthetic) targeted membrane, cytosolic, and endosomal receptors, arguing that the mode of activation is not driving the discrepancies in responder fates.
source: Moreover, various stimuli (live and synthetic) targeted membrane, cytosolic, and endosomal receptors, arguing that the mode of activation is not driving the discrepancies in responder fates.

claim: Quorum sensing triggers collective and coordinated actions in DCs activated in the draining lymph node, in vivo.

claim: Studies have reported that DC activation by Poly(I:C) harbors a collective production of IFN-I, which drives DC activation at the population level in vivo.
